entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

-    left out: they test the firmware, not the load path.

lines: # GitHub doesn't show as Verified, and never replaces a file a release
# already has. A tag config/releases.json doesn't list gets no release:
# the run says so in a notice and succeeds (the owner's answer,
-# 2026-10-26: m2 to m8 get no versions). It builds in the build image
-# pinned by registry digest (config/build-image) and publishes only a
-# release that names it (tools/release.py verify --publish).
+# 2026-10-26: m2 to m8 get no versions). Before it builds, it checks the
+# tag's build Dockerfile against the build's identity (config/build-image:
+# the base image's registry digest, the Dockerfile's and the toolchain's
+# SHA-256; the owner's answer, 2026-10-27), builds the image fresh from it
+# (never published), and publishes only a release that records that
+# identity (tools/release.py verify --publish).
name: release
on:
run: |
set -eu
version=$(python3 -c 'import json; print(json.load(open("release/release.json"))["version"])')
-          # Only a release built in the pinned build image (tools/release.py
-          # verify --publish checks the same): never a local dry run.
+          # Only a release that records the build's identity
+          # (tools/release.py verify --publish checks the same): never a
+          # local dry run.
container=$(python3 -c 'import json; print(json.load(open("release/release.json")).get("build", {}).get("container", ""))')
case "$container" in
-            *) echo "::error::build.container is '$container', not a pinned build image: not published"; exit 1 ;;
+            build-identity:*) ;;
+            *) echo "::error::build.container is '$container', not a build identity: not published"; exit 1 ;;
esac
if ! gh release view "$TAG" >/dev/null 2>&1; then

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98
"""Spec-side text discipline (R-SEP-1, check C-SEP-TERMS).
  check-emulator-terms.py [--show]
Looks for identifiers that occur in vendor/emulator/ and nowhere in
vendor/jieli-sdk/ or (since M4b) vendor/plaits/, in the places the firmware
side reads:
  - every tracked text file outside vendor/emulator/, harness/, sessions/
    (transcripts), docs/prompts/ (prompts are kept verbatim) and
    vendor/plaits/ (third-party code we didn't write, since M4b; its
    SOURCE.md, which we write, is scanned since SR-4);
  - the two doors, docs/HARNESS.md and docs/HARDWARE-SPEC.md, and their
    reviews in docs/reviews/, for identifier-shaped words only: they carry
    addresses and other numbers on purpose, each one sourced, and people
    review them too (R-SPEC-2);
  - the commit messages in COMMIT_RANGE (default ..HEAD);
  - the pull request's title and body, when GITHUB_EVENT_PATH names one.
The list is built at run time from vendor/emulator/ and never written down:
identifier-shaped words (with an underscore, inner capitals, or letters and
digits mixed; four characters or more, not just hex digits) and hex numbers
of four digits or more, except universal constants (powers of two, 2^n-1,
2^n+1, sign-bit masks and IEEE 754's standard patterns: universal(), by
rule, since SR-4's note). Terms that already occur in CLEAN_BASELINE's tree
(the repository as the clean side left it at the end of M0a, before any
emulator source entered it) or in vendor/jieli-sdk/ (whole identifiers, or the parts of one between
underscores) are not on the list. Since M4b (the owner's decision) neither
are the terms of vendor/plaits/, Mutable Instruments' Plaits, MIT, built
the same way as the SDK's, but only from the files vendor/plaits/SHA256SUMS
lists, each matching its hash (the pinned upstream tree, R-REPRO-7); if any
doesn't, the check fails. The output says how many emulator-only terms the
Plaits list takes off (a count, never the terms). A hit is reported as its place and a SHA-256 prefix of the word, never
the word or the text around it, because the log is visible to the firmware
side; `--show` prints the word too, for a spec-side author fixing it.
A hit is accepted without an entry of its own when the term occurs in one of
the two doors as they are on main (DOOR_FILES at origin/main, or at the
commit DOORS_REF names): what is there passed people's review. The doors are
read from that commit's blobs, never from the working tree, so a branch
cannot get a term accepted by adding it to a door; a term new to a door is
still a hit until the change that adds it has merged. When that commit
can't be found, nothing is accepted this way (and the output says so).
Any other reviewed false positive is listed by its hash in
config/emulator-terms-reviewed.json, with a reason that doesn't name it.
Where vendor/emulator/ isn't on disk (a clean folder), it says SKIP.
"""
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
---
name: ci-artifacts-named-files
description: "Clean side: a CI report artifact downloaded whole carries the record's harness/ folder; take named files only, and how to find and fix a C-SEP-TERMS hit"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: cd82f4be-e875-4959-b383-d66813d290ce
  modified: 2026-10-25T17:40:00.000Z
---

A `gh run download` of a CI report artifact brings the whole record, including its `harness/` folder of harness test results. M7 (2026-10-24) did that twice, opened only named logs, deleted both and recorded it in EXPOSURE.md.

**Why:** the clean-room rules let clean sessions take only named files of the firmware's own records; a whole artifact is the record wholesale.

**How to apply:**
- Read CI results from `gh run view <id> --log` first.
- If an artifact file is needed, name the file: ARP (2026-10-25) fetched the zip by API and ran `unzip -p zip logs/C-SEP-TERMS.log` (nothing else extracted), then deleted the zip at once and recorded it.
- C-SEP-TERMS gives only a place and a hash (`sha256(word)[:16]`). Hash the flagged line's words the same way to find the word.
- C-SEP-TERMS also scans commit messages and PR texts: a rename commit, PR text or EXPOSURE entry must never name the flagged word, or it fails again (ARP had to reword and force-push a commit).
- Pick names unlikely to be emulator identifiers (a plain `keys_*` name was one).
- A false positive goes in `config/emulator-terms-reviewed.json` by its own PR, which keeps a budget PR clean.

Related: [[provenance-ids-race]]

lines: # GitHub doesn't show as Verified, and never replaces a file a release
# already has. A tag config/releases.json doesn't list gets no release:
# the run says so in a notice and succeeds (the owner's answer,
-# 2026-10-26: m2 to m8 get no versions). It builds in the build image
-# pinned by registry digest (config/build-image) and publishes only a
-# release that names it (tools/release.py verify --publish).
+# 2026-10-26: m2 to m8 get no versions). Before it builds, it checks the
+# tag's build Dockerfile against the build's identity (config/build-image:
+# the base image's registry digest, the Dockerfile's and the toolchain's
+# SHA-256; the owner's answer, 2026-10-27), builds the image fresh from it
+# (never published), and publishes only a release that records that
+# identity (tools/release.py verify --publish).
name: release
on:
run: |
set -eu
version=$(python3 -c 'import json; print(json.load(open("release/release.json"))["version"])')
-          # Only a release built in the pinned build image (tools/release.py
-          # verify --publish checks the same): never a local dry run.
+          # Only a release that records the build's identity
+          # (tools/release.py verify --publish checks the same): never a
+          # local dry run.
container=$(python3 -c 'import json; print(json.load(open("release/release.json")).get("build", {}).get("container", ""))')
case "$container" in
-            *) echo "::error::build.container is '$container', not a pinned build image: not published"; exit 1 ;;
+            build-identity:*) ;;
+            *) echo "::error::build.container is '$container', not a build identity: not published"; exit 1 ;;
esac
if ! gh release view "$TAG" >/dev/null 2>&1; then

## Questions

1. **A blocked command will fail the next transcript check.** While resolving a merge conflict I sent an `ls` of the spec-side transcript folder. Claude Code's deny rule blocked it and it never ran, so nothing was listed or opened. It's not a false positive, though: it was an attempt. How do you want it recorded? I'd suggest a reviewed entry that says it was denied and never ran. It's already described in my EXPOSURE.md entry.
2. **What `build.container` means.** docs/M9-PLAN.md (the spec side's document) still describes it as "the build container's image digest". It now holds the build's identity. Should the spec side update that wording?
3. **fwtest images may not rebuild the same.** #142's merge pushed a second 0.7.0 image with digest `26102ae9…`, not the pinned `d7804526…`. Nothing here uses it, but it's for the spec side to look at.
4. **Which `.fwsc` should the app and web-build sessions test?** m1 predates A1, so there's no `.fm1img` and `.fwsc` pair from the same tag. A CI-built package from #153's branch is `out/a1/package/small-beeps-0.0.0.fwsc` (62 920 bytes, SHA-256 `27d1d60e…`). Should I put one in `drop/releases/`?

## What was done

- **Start:** the role file says `clean`. I archived clean-pin-answers. The transcript check flagged three of its calls, all `:!` exclusion pathspecs; each now has a reviewed entry for your approval, and the check passes. Your answer 2 is recorded in my EXPOSURE entry without changing the earlier lines. The prompt is saved unedited.
- **Pin fwtest 0.8.0 (#152):** the firmware suite (store cases included) and the ARP suite pass on both 0.7.0 and 0.8.0. Of 3 480 output files, nothing changed: the 633 that differ hold only fwtest's version and the runner line. `tests.test_store` OK.
  - My first 0.7.0 run didn't count: I switched branches while it was still building its test images. I reran it on a tree I left alone.
- **Build identity, your answer 1 (#151):** `config/build-image` now holds the base image's digest and the SHA-256 of `tools/Dockerfile` and of the toolchain.
  - In CI, `release.sh` checks the tag's Dockerfile against all three before it builds, then builds the image fresh (never published) and records the identity in `build.container`.
  - Tried by hand on m1: it built and passed `verify --publish`. With one digit of the Dockerfile hash changed, it stopped before building.
  - release.py, the workflow, RELEASING.md, TOOLCHAIN.md, PLAN.md and R-REL-3 are updated to match.
- **The A1 packager (#153):**
  - A second link of the same code at `0x02000120`. The raw `app.bin` is byte-identical to before.
  - `tools/fwsc.py` packs it (from HW-87 to HW-91 only, no loader files) and reads a package back with fwtest's nine checks in fwtest's own order and words.
  - New CI check C-PACKAGE: eight suite cases give identical outputs from the raw image and the package. The only differences are the startup data block, which matches HARNESS.md, and each path's own image on the flash chip. fwtest refuses all 12 broken packages with the reader's exact words.
  - Releases now include a `.fwsc` when the build has the package link.
  - CI first failed C-SEP-TERMS on four names I had chosen that also occur in the emulator's source; I renamed them. All four PRs now pass CI.
- **Dry run of m1:** made with main's tools; the record's tree hash was given as 64 zeros, a stand-in. It rebuilt m1's image byte for byte. The `.fm1img` is at `~/Development/<top>/drop/releases/small-beeps-0.1.0.fm1img` (SHA-256 `355208eb…`), a local dry run, never published.
- **The stand-in:** `stand-in.fm1img` passes all seven checks. It holds m1's exact image (`ee2ad8a0…`) but labels itself `0.9.0-dryrun.m1`. I read nothing else in that folder.

## Choices I made where the prompt left room
- **The eight "main cases":** boot, heartbeat, screen, keys, fmgold, midimsg, views and edit. Cases on test builds or generated flash files are left out.
- **The package's identity:** `small-beeps-<version>`, or just `small-beeps` when that would be over 19 characters.
- **The two-links check:** "same code in both links" applies to the firmware build only. The store's wipe test build turns a link address into a flash offset on purpose, so it differs.
- **Pushing:** git first refused to push because it wanted a branch tip this folder hadn't fetched. A plain fetch fixed it, and the barrier check afterwards found no spec-side files.

## Merge order
**#152 → #150 → #151 → #153.** #153 already contains #152 and #151.
